messages.subject: Putting draft pharmacometric functions on the Stan Github
parts:
The original post was in an e-mail chain, but here is a summary, and answer to some of the questions that have been asked.

My team is writing new functions for Stan with applications in Pharmacometrics. These functions can be called directly inside a stan file (so there is no dependence on whether the user uses cmdStan, PyStan, etc.)

We call this function library Torsten, after Torsten Teorell, who is regarded as the father of Pharmacokinetics.

The current code is compatible with stan/math-2.10.0.

The functions are coded in C++ and would be located in a directory under stan/math. So I expect to upload them in the stan-dev/math branch. The major advantage in doing so is that it will be easier to work on the code and get help on it, since it will be accessible to the community.

To expose some of these functions, I modified rev/mat.hpp and function_signatures.h. Other functions however are higher-order functions (to the same effect as integrate_ode_bdf and integrate_ode_rk45), and cannot simply be exposed in function_signatures.h. So I edited a few grammar files for the sole purpose of exposing these higher-order functions. I expect to share these modifications using the stan-dev/stan branch.

These higher-order functions have 14 arguments, which means we will need to increase the limit on the number of arguments (which is currently 12).

I still have to write unit tests, consistent with Stan practices. (I wrote some examples and tests using cmdStan and R, for development purposes but these are likely not consistent with Stan's practices. In due time, I will upload the examples to the stan/examples repo).

I agree with Bob's suggestion: we can start with a wiki and I am happy to attend a stan meeting to discuss design.

I hope this clarifies matter, and I'm happy to answer any other question.

parts:
This is really great news and I am very curious to see the solutions you have come up with.

In fact, I intended to start such a wiki on how to make Stan better/easier to use for PK/PD.

From my perspective we need a discussion on the design of things. I myself have come up with large Stan programs which can exactly do what I want - this is in my case to take a Nonmem data set and fit PK/PD models.

I intentionally kept things to be programmed in the Stan language only as I think that there should be no Nonmem (or PK/PD) specifics in Stan C++ and I am also not sure if we want to have PK model specifics in Stan (unless there are good arguments for it, of course).

From my experience in programming these models I figured it would probably make sense to include an event handling mechanism in Stan. In PK models it is crucial to code the dosing history of a given patient. To me it would be natural to include into Stan a facility (functions and possibly data-structures) which can handle these events for the purpose of making it easier to code and to speedup things. Such an event mechanism will probably be very useful for other domains as well aside from PK/PD models and the event handler may not be limited to ODE models, but should be able to cope with analytic models as well.

To move forward, we should definitely discuss during a Stan meeting. I guess we also need a wiki and maybe a scratch place to keep Thorsten code around and maybe my little Stan only solution. From there we should decide how to design things, what makes sense to include into Stan itself and what should live on the Stan language side.

Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Putting draft pharmacometric functions on the Stan Github
parts:
Hi Sebastian,

I'll set up a wiki so we can pool ideas, and will create a gitHub repo to post Thorsten. Once I have created the unit tests and dealt with forward auto-diff, I'll proceed to add the code to stan-dev.

Some quick thoughts:

The main benefit of using built-in stan functions is that the user does not need to write extensive code in the function block. I also imagine it would be pretty involved (if at all possible?) to write in Stan some of the code I did in C++ (I used classes and functors a lot...). Built-in functions make the coding more efficient and very easy, which I think will be key to interest users.

All the functions take in NONMEM data and return amounts in each compartment at each event. There are roughly speaking 4 functions. Here are two examples:

PKTwoCptModel() which analytically computes the solution to a two compartment model with first order absorption.

genCptModel_bdf() which computes the solution to an ODE system specified by a user using the integrate_ode_bdf function.

These functions all take advantage of exactly the same event handling mechanism, which augments the data and then sequentially predicts the amounts one event at a time. What changes from one function to the other is the function that predicts the amount at an individual event.

Right now the event mechanism is designed for NONMEM data, but I agree it would be great to generalize it. Maybe we could create a stan function that let's the user specify the one-event predictive function in the function block and then runs it sequentially through all the events.


Charles

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Putting draft pharmacometric functions on the Stan Github
parts:
Well, my Stan programs got ~1k lines long, but it works. So I was able to dump a NONMEM data set into Stan, then do some index fiddling to prepare the data for efficient traversal in what I call an event driver function.

A huge fraction of that code is completely agnostic to the specific model. In fact, the model function (be it an ODE or not) most be able to calculate the solutions for a given state of the compartments, the parameters and the initial time.

I was able to handle a 2-cmt oral dosing situation with time-changing clearance. It's tedious work to put that together and I guess things run faster if the event handling would be done by Stan.

For Stan I think we need a data-structure to represent events and a function to "execute" these events given a model. This would be very useful for many other domains as well and as such should not be Nonmem specific. Having such a data-structure would certainly allow to quickly convert Nonmem data to this structure. This is my view on this - and yes we should certainly pool our ideas on the wiki.

BTW, this event-thing could be used to include an event like "new-patient" or better "new grouping unit". This could then potentially in the long run enable a parallelized evaluation of the likelihood (given we figure out how to extend the nested AD to such a case which is doable from my understanding).

Sebastian

Sebastian,

Have you had an interaction with Wenping Wang and his work on PHXStan (also at Novartis but I appreciate a large organization). I was able to get ahold of the source code, (previously mentioned by Andrew http://andrewgelman.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/10/poster_PMXstan_ACoP2015_30Sep2015.pdf) however since it predated much of the ODE work they also implemented their own custom implementations, as well as some analytical solutions for the traditional 1cmpt/2 cmpt models.

Right now they want to keep the source "closed" until it gets cleaned up, however I am encouraging them to open it up to everyone, maybe this effort will be enough to throw that code into the ring as well.

I am finally getting through a swath of other projects (including my thesis work :-p) and will have time to start working this (and some cloudstan ideas) and am happy to contribute in some capacity.


Playing the devil's advocate a little, in regards to incorporating directly in stan/math, unless the functions are generic (in application) I wonder as to the potentially slippery slope of industry-specific code being "dumped" into that repo. Pharmacometrics alone has so many somewhat niche (at least in terms of design) needs in terms of things like events I wonder if some sort of independent module would be more appropriate and provide an example path forward for other industries interested in substantial domain-specific code.

Charles, have you interacted much with Kyle regarding how he is managing events and such in mrgsolve. As a DSL, mrgsolve has been very pleasant for simulation and could be a nice to have a reasonably aligned API. https://github.com/mrgsolve and docs https://github.com/metrumresearchgroup/mrgsolve/wiki/gallery

messages.author: 5a7d96b840c23bef
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Putting draft pharmacometric functions on the Stan Github
parts:
While we (Charles and I) have built some prototype pharmacometrics (PMX) functions in C++, I'm pretty agnostic about the Stan language vs C++ issue. I agree that certain core functionality should be part of Stan math like numerical solvers for systems of ODEs and algebraic equations and some sort of event handling like that suggested by Sebastian. The more PMX-specific functions could be either C++ or Stan language. I look forward to further discussion about which approach may be optimal or most consistent with Stan design philosophy.

What is missing is some convenient way to distribute and install domain-specific functionality, e.g., some sort of package distribution mechanism ala CRAN or even just being able to include external files containing Stan language functions. In the absence of that, I prefer to have the PMX functions incorporated into Stan so they are easily distributed as part of the standard Stan distribution.

Cheers,
Bill

I was wondering the same thing about lots of domain-specific
code. It's a real tradeoff. By including it directly in stan::math,
everything stays compatible because we agree to maintain it. And it's
easy for everyone to install and access. This is convenient, but
a heavy long-term commitment. And it means everything just takes longer
in stan::lang and stan::math, like unit testing.

This one's a bit trickier because it involves modifying the parser.
I don't see how to make that extensible. Just a bunch of function
libraries would be easy to include, but parser code is pretty entangled
with the rest of the Stan language because of the recursion
through expressions (or statements).

Hmm. I'll add it as a meeting discussion topic.

- Bob

I agree that certain core functionality should be part of Stan math like numerical solvers for systems of ODEs and algebraic equations and some sort of event handling like that suggested by Sebastian. The more PMX-specific functions could be either C++ or Stan language. I look forward to further discussion about which approach may be optimal or most consistent with Stan design philosophy.

That philosophy is a work in progress. Requirements change as we
add more users and more developers and more interfaces and add-ons.
Dependencies are the bane of all computational work.

> What is missing is some convenient way to distribute and install domain-specific functionality, e.g., some sort of package distribution mechanism ala CRAN or even just being able to include external files containing Stan language functions. In the absence of that, I prefer to have the PMX functions incorporated into Stan so they are easily distributed as part of the standard Stan distribution.

Exactly. That's what I meant by figuring out some general
way to extend Stan.

Unless you code analytic gradients or want to use fancy C++
features like template metaprogramming, it's just as efficient
to code in Stan as in C++. But we need a general way to extend
Stan programs, too. There's a placeholder in R, but we want
to make a general include mechanism.

And double exactly on making it easy on users to install. The
more hurdles users have to jump through, the less likely they
will be to install or upgrade.

- Bob
